issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Thinking: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
issues.explanation: The denial/minimisation in Magical Thinking sits awkwardly with the very global, entrenched negative self-change appraisals. A patient who mainly copes by telling himself the event did not really happen or was not that bad would not typically also report such strongly elaborated identity-collapse appraisals unless there were clearer supporting items linking the trauma to guilt/shame; here the combination feels internally strained.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
issues.explanation: For trauma type 'accidentally caused serious injury to another', the negative appraisals are missing the expected guilt/responsibility/being dangerous-to-others theme. Instead they focus on global misery and identity change, which is not impossible but is a weak fit to the trauma-specific cognitive content.

vignette: Diego's hands still tremble when he thinks about that day on the job site. He was a young HVAC technician, barely out of his apprenticeship, when an accident involving a faulty valve left one of his coworkers with serious burns. The memory of the sound of screams and the smell of charred skin has stayed with him ever since. Over time, Diego has come to believe that his body is unreliable, that it can betray him at any moment - just like it did on that day. As a result, he's become increasingly withdrawn, only feeling safe in a limited number of places, such as his small apartment or the familiar surroundings of his family's home. Unusual silence makes him feel like something dangerous is about to happen, and he often finds himself checking and re-checking his tools and equipment before starting work, trying to avoid any potential stressors that could lead to another accident. He avoids anniversaries connected to the event, not wanting to relive the horror of that day. Diego's mind constantly replays the details of the accident, trying to make sense of what happened and how he could have prevented it. This overanalysing has become a vicious cycle, leading him to feel even more guilty about his inaction during the emergency. He is certain that he will never forgive himself for not doing more to stop what happened, and this self-blame has only intensified his feelings of guilt and shame. The memory of the accident feels alien to Diego, like it belongs to someone else rather than him. When he thinks about it, he can sometimes smell the acrid scent of burned skin and ozone, transporting him back to that moment on the job site. The memory forces its way into his mind when he least expects it, triggered by sounds or smells that remind him of the accident. As Diego navigates his daily routine, these memories trigger strong physical reactions - a racing heart, sweating palms, and an overwhelming sense of anxiety. His body's response to these triggers has become so intense that he's started to believe that even in silence, something is waiting to pounce on him. This perception of threat only reinforces his negative self-appraisals, making him feel like the person he's become is unrecognisable to himself. The consequences of Diego's avoidance behaviours have been significant - he's had to turn down lucrative job opportunities because they involve working with similar equipment or in environments that remind him of the accident. His relationships with friends and family have also suffered, as he's withdrawn from social gatherings and events that might trigger memories of that day. Despite his best efforts to move on, Diego remains trapped in a cycle of guilt, shame, and anxiety, unable to shake off the memory of what happened. As the anniversary of the accident approaches, Diego finds himself becoming increasingly agitated, feeling like he's losing control once again. He knows he needs help to break free from this cycle, but his fear of confronting the past has held him back until now. With a deep sense of trepidation, Diego has finally decided to seek professional help, hoping that therapy can help him come to terms with what happened and find a way to forgive himself.
